t: Nomen, Genus und Artikel (Nouns, Gender and Article)
d: Level: A1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Know that every German noun has a gender, learn to store nouns with their article, and learn the patterns that let you guess gender correctly most of the time. Why this matters This is the most important lesson in A1. Everything later depends on it: Akkusativ, Dativ, adjective endings, relative pronouns. All of it needs the gender. English speakers often learn Tisch = table and move on. That is the mistake that causes a wall at B1. Learn der Tisch from the start. It costs the same effort now and saves enormous pain later. --- Material Every noun has a gender German nouns are masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). This is grammatical gender, not biological, and it is largely arbitrary. das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter. der Löffel (the spoon) is masculine. There is no logic to fix by thinking harder. Article Gender Example --- --- --- der masculine der Tisch (table), der Mann (man), der Tag (day) die feminine die Tür (door), die Frau (woman), die Zeit (time) das neuter das Kind (child), das Buch (book), das Haus (house) The plural article is always die Singular Plural --- --- der Tisch die Tische die Tür die Türen das Kind die Kinder Whatever the singular gender, the plural article is always die. This is the one piece of good news. How to write vocabulary from now on Never write a no

This is pure survival German and it appears in every exam and every shop. Why this matters Numbers and time are the vocabulary you cannot avoid. Level: A1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Understand what a case is, recognise the accusative (the direct object), and change articles correctly in the accusative. Why this matters This is the second most important lesson in A1, after gender. German marks the role of a noun in the sentence by changing its article. The accusative is the first case you meet, and it is the gateway to Dativ, Genitiv, and every adjective ending later. Good news: the accusative is the easiest case. Only the masculine article changes. Feminine, neuter, and plural look exactly the same as the nominative. --- Material What is a case? A case shows the function of a noun in the sentence: is it the doer, the receiver, or something else? Case Function Question Example --- --- --- --- Nominativ Subject (the doer) Wer? Was? Der Mann kauft ein Auto. Akkusativ Direct object (the receiver) Wen? Was? Ich sehe den Mann. Dativ Indirect object Wem? Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch. Genitiv Possession Wessen? Das Auto des Mannes. At A1 you need Nominativ and Akkusativ. Dativ comes at A2. The accusative change Only masculine changes. der becomes den. Everything else stays. Gender Nominative Accusative Change? --- --- --- --- Masculine der den Yes Feminine die die No Neuter das das No Plural die die No Articles in the accusative Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural --- --- --- --- ---

Level: A1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Use the six modal verbs to talk about ability, necessity, permission, and wishes, and understand the special word order they create. Why this matters Modal verbs are everywhere in real German. Kannst du...? (Can you...?), Ich muss... (I must...), Ich möchte... (I would like...) are the backbone of everyday requests. They also teach you the Satzklammer (sentence bracket), which is a core German structure. --- Material The six modal verbs Verb Meaning Nuance --- --- --- können can, to be able to Ability or possibility müssen must, to have to Necessity, obligation wollen to want Strong intention möchten would like Polite wish (technically Konjunktiv II of mögen) dürfen may, to be allowed to Permission sollen should, ought to Recommendation, duty, someone else's instruction mögen (to like) also exists and is related to möchten, but at A1 you mainly need möchten for polite requests. Conjugation Modal verbs are irregular. Notice: no ending in the ich and er/sie/es forms. Person können müssen wollen möchten dürfen sollen --- --- --- --- --- --- --- ich kann muss will möchte darf soll du kannst musst willst möchtest darfst sollst er/sie/es kann muss will möchte darf soll wir können müssen wollen möchten dürfen sollen ihr könnt müsst wollt möchtet dürft sollt sie/Sie können müssen wollen möchten dürfe

Level: A1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Build correct German sentences: statements, questions, and negations. Understand why the verb is almost always in position 2, and how to move other elements around it. Why this matters German word order is rigid compared to English, and it is one of the most noticeable markers of a learner. English lets you move things around freely; German does not. But the rule is simple once you see it: the verb is the second element, always, in a statement. Master this and your German instantly sounds much better. --- Material The three positions German sentences are analysed as: Position 1 Position 2 (verb) Position 3+ --- --- --- Ich lerne Deutsch. Heute lerne ich Deutsch. Deutsch lerne ich heute. The verb never leaves position 2 in a simple statement. Whatever you put in position 1 (subject, time, place, object), the verb follows immediately. Statements: verb in position 2 Ich trinke Kaffee. (I drink coffee.) Heute trinke ich Kaffee. (Today I drink coffee.) — Time first, verb still second, subject moves after. Kaffee trinke ich jeden Morgen. (Coffee I drink every morning.) — Object first, same rule. This is called V2 (verb-second) word order. It is the fundamental rule. Questions: two types Yes/no questions (Ja/Nein-Fragen): verb first. German English --- --- Trinkst du Kaffee? Do you drink coffee? Ist

Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Understand the dative case, change articles and pronouns correctly, and learn the prepositions and verbs that always take the dative. Why this matters This is the most important lesson in A2, exactly as gender was in A1. The dative appears constantly: after certain verbs (helfen, gefallen), after certain prepositions (mit, nach, bei), and as the indirect object. If A1 taught you that articles change, A2 teaches you there is a second set of changes. Good news: the dative has more changes than the accusative, but they follow a pattern you can memorise in one table. --- Material The accusative vs the dative Case Function Question Example --- --- --- --- Nominativ Subject Wer? Was? Der Mann liest. Akkusativ Direct object Wen? Was? Ich sehe den Mann. Dativ Indirect object Wem? Ich helfe dem Mann. Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch. — I give the man the book. dem Mann = dative (the receiver), das Buch = accusative (the thing given). Definite articles in the dative Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural --- --- --- --- --- Nominative der die das die Akkusativ den die das die Dativ dem der dem den + noun gets -n Two things to notice: 1. Feminine changes to der in the dative. So der appears twice, but means different things. 2. Plural adds -n to the noun: die Kinder → den Kindern, die Freunde → den Freunden. Indefi

Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Handle verbs that take two objects, put them in the correct order, and use the right pronoun forms. Why this matters This is where the dative earns its keep. Sentences like Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch have both cases in one sentence. Getting the order right (person before thing) is a core German skill, and it appears in every exam. --- Material Verbs with two objects These verbs take a dative person and an accusative thing. Verb English Example --- --- --- geben to give Ich gebe dem Kind (D) den Ball (A). bringen to bring Er bringt mir (D) das Buch (A). kaufen to buy (for someone) Ich kaufe dir (D) ein Geschenk (A). schenken to give as a gift Sie schenkt ihm (D) eine Uhr (A). zeigen to show Zeig mir (D) den Weg (A). schicken to send Ich schicke ihr (D) eine E-Mail (A). erklären to explain Er erklärt uns (D) die Regel (A). empfehlen to recommend Ich empfehle Ihnen (D) das Restaurant (A). sagen to say (to someone) Ich sage dir (D) die Wahrheit (A). leihen to lend Leihst du mir (D) dein Auto (A)? vorstellen to introduce Ich stelle Ihnen (D) meinen Kollegen (A) vor. wünschen to wish Ich wünsche dir (D) viel Glück (A). The golden rule: person before thing When both objects are nouns, the order is dative (person) first, then accusative (thing). Ich gebe dem Mann (D) das Buch (A). ✅ Ich gebe das Buch

Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Talk about the past using the Perfekt tense, and know when to use haben and when to use sein as the helper verb. Why this matters This is the biggest new skill in A2. Without the past tense, you cannot tell anyone what you did, which blocks almost every real conversation. The Perfekt is the spoken past tense in German. If you are talking, you use Perfekt, not Präteritum. --- Material How the Perfekt is built The Perfekt has two parts, which form a Satzklammer (sentence bracket): Helper verb (haben or sein) in position 2 + Partizip II at the end. Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt. (I have yesterday German learned = I learned German yesterday.) Structure: Subject + haben/sein + ... + Partizip II. haben or sein? The core decision Use sein with: 1. Movement from A to B: gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen, reisen, fahren 2. Change of state: werden (to become), einschlafen (to fall asleep), aufwachen (to wake up), sterben (to die), aufstehen (to get up), wachsen (to grow) 3. Three important exceptions: sein (been), bleiben (stayed), passieren (happened) Use haben with: - Everything else. Most verbs. Especially all transitive verbs (verbs with an accusative object). Memory aid: sein verbs are "movement or change". Think of a person physically moving from one place to another, or transforming. Eve

Why this matters The helper verb (haben/sein) is easy. The Partizip II is the hard part, because German has strong (irregular) verbs with unpredictable forms. This lesson gives you the patterns, so you can form most participles and recognise the rest. --- Material Regular (weak) verbs: ge- + stem + -t Infinitive Partizip II English --- --- --- lernen gelernt learned machen gemacht made, did kaufen gekauft bought spielen gespielt played arbeiten gearbeitet worked wohnen gewohnt lived hören gehört heard sagen gesagt said fragen gefragt asked kochen gekocht cooked Verbs ending in -t or -d add an extra e: arbeiten → gearbeitet, reden → geredet. Irregular (strong) verbs: ge- + changed stem + -en Infinitive Partizip II English --- --- --- gehen gegangen gone kommen gekommen come sehen gesehen seen lesen gelesen read essen gegessen eaten trinken getrunken drunk sprechen gesprochen spoken schreiben geschrieben written fahren gefahren driven fliegen geflogen flown nehmen genommen taken geben gegeben given finden gefunden found singen gesungen sung schlafen geschlafen slept helfen geholfen helped treffen getroffen met bleiben geblieben stayed sein gewesen been Notice: stron

t: Nebensätze mit weil, dass, wenn, ob
d: Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Build subordinate clauses (Nebensätze) with the verb at the end, using the four most common subordinating conjunctions. Why this matters This is the third big jump in A2. Up to now, every sentence had the verb in position 2. Subordinate clauses break that rule: the verb goes to the end. This is one of the most characteristic features of German, and getting it right is a major milestone. Once you can say Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will, you can express reasons, opinions, and conditions. That is real communication. --- Material The rule: verb at the end In a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the very end. Main clause Conjunction Subordinate clause --- --- --- Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will. Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt. Ich komme, wenn ich Zeit habe. Ich frage, ob er Zeit hat. Compare: Ich will in Deutschland arbeiten. (main clause, verb position 2) ..., weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will. (subordinate, verb last) The four conjunctions Conjunction Meaning Use --- --- --- weil because Gives a reason dass that Reports information, thoughts, opinions wenn when, if Conditions, repeated events ob whether Indirect yes/no questions weil (because) Answers the question "Warum?" (Why?). Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeit

Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Connect clauses correctly with coordinating and subordinating conjunctions, and know which ones change the word order and which do not. Why this matters Conjunctions turn short sentences into real speech. Without them, you sound like a textbook: Ich lerne Deutsch. Ich will arbeiten. Ich mag Deutschland. With them: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten will, und ich mag das Land. This is the difference between A1 and A2 output. --- Material Three groups of connectors German connectors fall into three groups, based on what happens to the word order. Group Position of verb Examples --- --- --- Coordinating (Position 0) Normal order, no change und, aber, oder, denn, sondern Subordinating Verb goes to the end weil, dass, wenn, ob, obwohl, damit Adverbial (Position 1) Verb stays position 2, subject follows deshalb, trotzdem, dann, also This is the key insight: the connector's type determines the word order. Group 1: Coordinating conjunctions (no word order change) These sit in "position 0", before the clause. The clause keeps normal order. Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 5 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Put the correct ending on an adjective that comes before a noun, in all three patterns. Why this matters This is the most feared topic in German grammar, but it is mostly memorisation, not logic. Once you see that it is a table with three patterns, it becomes mechanical. The reason adjectives change is simple: the article sometimes does not show the gender clearly, so the adjective has to carry the information instead. German never leaves the noun's gender ambiguous. Relax. Even native speakers do not think about this consciously. Learn the three tables, drill them, and they become automatic. Getting it slightly wrong is common and usually still understood. --- Material The three patterns There are three situations, depending on what comes before the adjective: Pattern What comes before Example --- --- --- Weak der / die / das, dieser, jener der gute Wein Mixed ein / kein / mein (possessives) ein guter Wein Strong nothing (no article) guter Wein Why the ending changes The gender must be visible somewhere. If the article already shows it (der), the adjective can be lazy and just add -e. If there is no article, the adjective must show the full gender, so it looks like der/die/das itself: guter, gute, gutes. Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Use reflexive verbs and reflexive pronouns correctly, in both the accusative and the dative. Why this matters Reflexive verbs are extremely common in German: sich freuen, sich interessieren, sich treffen, sich fühlen. Many everyday ideas use them, and some German reflexive verbs have no reflexive equivalent in English, so you cannot translate word by word. --- Material What a reflexive verb is A reflexive verb's action reflects back on the subject: the subject and object are the same person. Ich wasche mich. (I wash myself.) Er freut sich. (He is happy. Lit. "He pleases himself".) The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject, like any object pronoun. Reflexive pronouns (accusative) Most reflexive verbs use the accusative. Person Reflexive pronoun --- --- ich mich du dich er/sie/es sich wir uns ihr euch sie/Sie sich Ich wasche mich. Du wäschst dich. Er wäscht sich. Wir waschen uns. Reflexive pronouns (dative) Some verbs use the dative reflexive pronoun, usually because there is already an accusative object. Person Dative reflexive --- --- ich mir du dir er/sie/es sich wir uns ihr euch sie/Sie sich Notice: only ich and du differ (mir/dir vs mich/dich). The rest are the same. When is it dative? Why this matters Possessives are everywhere in daily speech: my family, your job, his car, our house. The tricky part is that German possessives change ending depending on the case and the gender of the owned noun, not the owner. --- Material The possessive stems Each person has a possessive stem. Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Give commands, instructions, requests, and advice in the correct form for each person. Why this matters The imperative is everyday German: instructions, recipes, directions, requests, warnings. It also appears in exams (writing instructions, giving advice) and in reading (signs, manuals). It is short and useful. --- Material Four forms of the imperative German has imperatives for du, ihr, Sie, and wir. Person Form Example (machen) --- --- --- du stem (often no ending) Mach! ihr stem + t Macht! Sie infinitive + Sie Machen Sie! wir infinitive + wir Machen wir! The du-form Take the du-present form, remove the -st ending, and drop the pronoun. Infinitive du-present Imperative (du) --- --- --- machen du machst Mach! lernen du lernst Lern! kommen du kommst Komm! gehen du gehst Geh! spielen du spielst Spiel! Level: A2 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Express when, how long, how often, and since when, using the correct prepositions and cases. Why this matters Time expressions are everywhere, and German has precise rules for each one. Using the wrong preposition (seit vs vor vs für) is one of the most common learner errors, and it is tested in exams. --- Material The four key prepositions Preposition Meaning Case Example --- --- --- --- seit since, for (ongoing) Dativ seit einem Jahr vor ago, before Dativ vor einer Woche für for (a duration, future) Akkusativ für zwei Wochen in in (future time) Dativ in einer Woche The crucial distinction: - seit = something started in the past and is still going on. Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch. (I have been learning German for a year, and still am.) - vor = a point in the past, counted back from now. Vor einer Woche war ich krank. In einer Woche habe ich Urlaub. (In a week I have vacation.) Common error: English speakers say "I have been learning German for a year" and use für. German uses seit for ongoing situations. Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 2 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Know when to use the Perfekt and when to use the Präteritum, and stop mixing them randomly. Why this matters You learned both tenses at A2. At B1, the question is no longer "how do I form it" but "which one do I choose". German speakers make this choice automatically and consistently, and using the wrong one sounds distinctly foreign. This is also tested in the writing module. --- Material The core rule Tense Where it is used Example --- --- --- Perfekt Spoken German, informal writing, personal letters Ich habe gestern einen Film gesehen. Präteritum Written German, narrative, formal reports Er ging zur Tür und öffnete sie. The short version: in speech, use the Perfekt. In writing, use the Präteritum. Without it, you cannot say "after I had done X, I did Y". --- Material What the Plusquamperfekt is It expresses an action that happened before another past action. In English, it is "had done". Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich spazieren. (After I had eaten, I went for a walk.) Two events: eating (first, Plusquamperfekt) → walking (second, Präteritum). Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Form and use the passive voice in the present, past, and with modal verbs. Why this matters The passive is everywhere in formal, official, technical, and news German: rules, procedures, announcements, reports. Without it you cannot read a German contract, instruction manual, or news article comfortably. It is a core B1 exam topic. --- Material What the passive is Active: the subject does the action. Der Arzt untersucht den Patienten. (The doctor examines the patient.) Passive: the action happens to the subject; the doer is backgrounded or dropped. Der Patient wird (vom Arzt) untersucht. Important: in the Perfekt and Plusquamperfekt, the passive uses worden (not geworden). worden is the passive form; geworden is used when werden means "to become" as a main verb. Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Express wishes, hypotheses, and polite requests using hätte, wäre, würde, and the other Konjunktiv II forms. Why this matters The Konjunktiv II is how German says "would", "could", "if I were", and "I wish". It is essential for politeness (Könnten Sie...?) and for hypotheticals (Wenn ich Zeit hätte...). It appears constantly in everyday speech and in exams. --- Material What the Konjunktiv II is It expresses something that is not real: wishes, hypotheses, polite requests, unreal conditions. Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich reisen. (If I were rich, I would travel.) Könnten Sie mir helfen? (Could you help me?) The situation is unreal or uncertain, unlike the indicative. The two ways to form it Method 1: the original Konjunktiv II forms (from the Präteritum + umlaut). Used mostly for haben, sein, modal verbs, and a few strong verbs. Method 2: würde + Infinitiv. Used for most other verbs. The most important forms (memorise these) Verb Konjunktiv II --- --- sein wäre haben hätte werden würde können könnte müssen müsste dürfen dürfte sollen sollte wollen wollte mögen möchte These nine cover the majority of everyday Konjunktiv II use. Learn them cold. Conjugation of sein (wäre) and haben (hätte) Person sein (wäre) haben (hätte) --- --- --- ich wäre hätte du wärst hättest er/sie/es wäre hätte wir wären

Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 3 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Express unreal situations in the past: "would have done", "if I had known", "I should have...". Why this matters This is how German expresses regret, reproach, and unreal past conditions: "If I had known, I would have come." It appears in exams, in formal writing, and in everyday conversation about the past. It builds directly on the Plusquamperfekt. --- Material What the Konjunktiv II past is It expresses something that did not happen in the past but was imagined, wished, or regretted. Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich gekommen. (If I had known that, I would have come.) Reality: I did not know, so I did not come. The sentence imagines the unreal alternative. How to form it hätte / wäre + Partizip II This is exactly the Plusquamperfekt form (hatte/war + Partizip II), but with hätte/wäre instead of hatte/war. Conjugation Person hätte + Partizip wäre + Partizip --- --- --- ich hätte gemacht wäre gegangen du hättest gemacht wärst gegangen er/sie/es hätte gemacht wäre gegangen wir hätten gemacht wären gegangen ihr hättet gemacht wärt gegan

Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 4 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Build relative clauses in the nominative, accusative, and dative, with the verb at the end. Why this matters Relative clauses let you add information about a noun without starting a new sentence: "the man who lives next door", "the book that I read". They are essential for any complex description, for writing, and for the speaking exam. The verb-at-the-end word order is the main challenge. --- Material What a relative clause is It describes a noun from the main clause, using a relative pronoun. Der Mann, der neben mir wohnt, ist Lehrer. (The man who lives next to me is a teacher.) der Mann = the noun being described (the Bezugswort). der = the relative pronoun. neben mir wohnt = the relative clause, verb at the end. The core rules 1. The relative clause follows the noun it describes. 2. It is separated by commas. 3. The relative pronoun agrees with the noun in gender and number. 4. The case of the relative pronoun depends on its function inside the relative clause. 5. The verb goes to the end of the relative clause. Level: B1 Target time: 30 minutes, repeat over 2 sessions Status: not started --- Goal Use Futur I for future plans, predictions, promises, and assumptions. Why this matters German often expresses the future with the present tense plus a time word (Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin). But Futur I (werden + infinitive) is essential for predictions, promises, assumptions, and emphasis. It is tested in exams, and it appears in news and formal writing. --- Material How to form it werden (conjugated) + infinitive (at the end) Person werden Example --- --- --- ich werde Ich werde kommen. du wirst Du wirst kommen. er/sie/es wird Er wird kommen. wir werden Wir werden kommen. ihr werdet Ihr werdet kommen. sie/Sie werden Sie werden kommen. Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren. (I will go to Berlin tomorrow.) When to use Futur I Use Example --- --- Prediction Es wird morgen regnen. Promise Ich werde dir helfen.
